headline: A 2014 law extends federal traumatic brain injury (TBI) programs through fiscal year 2019 and asks HHS and CDC to improve coordination and review research.
what_it_does: The law renews several federal TBI programs through fiscal year 2019, including prevention and tracking (surveillance or registry) programs. It also renews grants to states and Indian consortia for TBI services, and funding for protection and advocacy systems that help people with TBI. It directs the Department of Health and Human Services to build a plan for better coordination of federal TBI work, including feedback from people with TBI and their caregivers. It also directs the CDC to review scientific evidence on managing brain injuries in children and identify research opportunities.

who_it_affects.group: People with traumatic brain injury and their caregivers
who_it_affects.how: They may receive services through state and tribal grant programs and protection and advocacy systems that the law keeps funded through fiscal year 2019, and they are asked to give input on the federal coordination plan.

who_it_affects.group: State and tribal health agencies and Indian consortia
who_it_affects.how: They can keep receiving federal grants for TBI services through fiscal year 2019.
Their federal authorization to serve individuals with TBI is extended through fiscal year 2019.

who_it_affects.group: Children with brain injuries and their families
who_it_affects.how: The CDC must review evidence on brain injury management in children, which could guide future research, though the law does not itself change their care.

when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on November 26, 2014; the program reauthorizations run through fiscal year 2019.
